text:

If you're raising this year, that second look is the one we design for.

author: Ivan Shmalenko
headline: Co-founder at übernatural · Premium websites in 72 hours
title: Asking AI to change one headline
text:
Asking AI to change one headline on your homepage:

I use AI every day and I love the technology. But this happens quite often.

You ask it to change something on the homepage, and it goes and changes pieces on other pages you never mentioned.

And unless someone checks every page, nobody notices until the numbers drop.

A human team understands the scope of what you asked. And when something does go wrong, you know exactly who is responsible, legally and in practice.

That's why every day of a project we show the client what we delivered that day.

author: Ivan Shmalenko
headline: Co-founder at übernatural · Premium websites in 72 hours
title: Flights booked, no deal signed
text:
Telling my co-founder I booked flights for tomorrow. No deal signed yet:

This was a real Thursday.

An existing client referred us to his brother. On the call I started digging into the scope and the timeline, and I understood this could not be done online.

So I booked flights and a hotel for Friday, and texted everyone we knew in that country: let's catch up, we'll be here Friday to Monday.

For Bogdan, my co-founder, this was an insane decision. Then that evening I realised our visas had expired.

We applied online. They got approved while we slept.

Everybody we texted had time to meet on the weekend. We closed one ministry, it referred us to another, then another.

One referral became six clients. Five of them are government ministries.

Bogdan still accounts for every risk in the company, and I still book the flights. A government or a funded startup with a hard deadline gets both of us.

author: Ivan Shmalenko
headline: Co-founder at übernatural · Premium websites in 72 hours
title: What 'AI built this' videos leave out
text:
Hundreds of accounts post websites with one caption: Claude built this.

A few of those sites were designed and built by my team.

We use AI on client work every day, so here are the parts those videos leave out.

The failed attempts. One usable image usually takes four or five prompt tries.

The designer upstream. Many prompt sites sell prompts that were built from real designs. I sell my designs to a couple of them myself, paid and credited.

The defects. AI B-roll can put you in a different room between two cuts. Claude misses it, while anyone with some video production experience sees it.

Two checks before you believe a demo. Is there a screen recording of the whole process, start to finish? And whose design went in before the prompt?

A real site like the ones in those videos is much closer to $30,000 to $50,000 per project.

author: Ivan Shmalenko
headline: Co-founder at übernatural · Premium websites in 72 hours
title: A $2,000 editor beats Claude's tokens
text:
A decent video editor costs about $2,000 a month. In my tests, that's cheaper than Claude's tokens.

I kept seeing videos that said AI edited this from start to finish.

So I installed everything I needed and tried it myself. Without a ton of correction, it just doesn't work. It doesn't do what you want it to do.

The one place it helped was B-roll for a launch video we're making. Claude generated it in the background while I worked on other stuff.

I could use around 20% of it.

The rest had defects Claude did not see. The shot was clearly in a very different room, sometimes with a different person. Anyone with some video production experience sees that instantly.

Deciding what belongs in the frame is still a human job.

That's how our studio uses AI on client sites too. A designer does all the base design work, and AI generates the specific assets that design calls for.

author: Ivan Shmalenko
headline: Co-founder at übernatural · Premium websites in 72 hours
title: Lovable went from $100M to $600M a year
text:
A million new projects a week are now built on Lovable, the app builder you prompt.

Its annualized revenue passed $600M in September, up from $100M in July 2025. Two thirds of the Fortune 500 have users on it.

I think for launching fast, this is probably the best thing a founder can do. Launching fast is always the most important thing.

What I watch is the other side.

Anything AI builds fully on its own has a fingerprint. Claude Design got better, but it overuses a specific set of elements, and anyone who has seen a lot of those sites spots it.

The moment a buyer spots it, the product feels less valuable.

My read, and it is pattern recognition, not a measured fact: a million projects a week means a lot more sites that look like each other. That makes looking different more expensive, and worth more.

Founders, when you land on a website, what's the first thing that tells you it came from a prompt?

title: Midjourney: $0 raised, everyone has it
text:
Midjourney has never raised a dollar from investors.

Sacra estimates it made about $200M in 2023 with a team of around 40 people. Anyone can start for $10 a month.

So everyone has access to the same tool.

On our side, one usable image takes around four or five prompt tries and 20 to 30 generations. Then it goes through an upscaler and Photoshop to remove the AI artifacts, before a designer places it on the page.

Image generation is extremely overpowered if you have taste. If you understand 3D, how to shoot and edit video, how to draw.

Without that design input, you get AI slop, however many images you generate.

That's the part clients pay a studio for: the eye that picks the one image out of 30.

author: Ivan Shmalenko
headline: Co-founder at übernatural · Premium websites in 72 hours
title: AI keeps moving the goalpost
text:
AI keeps moving the goalpost for web design.

Something you could have sold four or five years ago is basically unsellable now, because AI can make it quite simply.

The same tools work in the other direction too.

Things that used to need a big agency with lots of different talent, a small experienced team can create now.

I can look at what we produced one year ago and what we produce right now. What we make now is tenfold better.

Firstly, because our team became much, much better. Secondly, because the tools became better, so the same talent produces even crazier outcomes.

And unless a client is a designer themselves, they cannot reliably produce a site like that on their own.

So if you're a founder judging your site against what looked premium two years ago, you're using a bar that has already moved.

author: Ivan Shmalenko
headline: Co-founder at übernatural · Premium websites in 72 hours
title: Your homepage has 50 milliseconds
text:
People judge a website in about 50 milliseconds.

That's a 2006 study by Lindgaard and colleagues. Google's own research later measured first impressions forming in 17 to 50 milliseconds.

My design account on Instagram passed 30 million views in two years. Every video there is just my team's design work.

Two years of that left me with one rule. The design should be interactive, things should be moving, it should feel immersive.

The same rule decides a website hero.

One caveat I always give. If you sell to cold traffic from ads, load speed matters most, and animation should never stand between a buyer and the checkout.

Most of our clients sell through calls and demos. For a warm prospect, the first second is where your company starts to feel premium.

title: How should an AI startup stand out?
text:
My honest answer to this has two parts.

The second one is more useful.

A lot of AI startups take their visual cues from other AI startups. That's how nature landscapes ended up on so many AI homepages.

So we start from the roots of the industry. Its history, the era when it was doing its best, the idea underneath the product.

We don't count it properly, but around 70 to 80% of the time the client picks the direction we were rooting for.

When they pick the other one, we don't push back much. The founder runs the company, and 90% of the time they understand their market better than we do.

headline: Team Lead Designer at übernatural · 400+ websites, 3 Awwwards
title: The Claude Design fingerprint
text:
Every site Claude Design makes carries the same tell.
I remove it on every project we ship.

One huge headline next to tiny uppercase text. Thin outlines around everything.

Once you've seen one site made by it, you've seen them all. Every AI tool has its own tells like this.

Anthropic launched Claude Design in April and says it can apply your design system to every project automatically. I still get that pairing on every page it gives me.

The fix is one instruction: drop the uppercase, change the composition.

Someone less experienced doesn't even know it's a cliche, because they haven't built up that much visual literacy yet.

At übernatural the font pairing, the colours and the overall style come from a person. The model gets the assembly.

So if your homepage has the giant font and the tiny caps, now you know where it came from.

author: Egor Galiy
headline: Team Lead Designer at übernatural · 400+ websites, 3 Awwwards
title: When Claude does the opposite of the prompt
text:
Some weeks Claude does the exact opposite of my prompt.
So I move the whole project to Cursor.

It looks like this. I give it a task, and it's already doing the opposite.

There's no clever signal behind the switch. It's purely a gut feeling, when there's a really obvious failure to do the task.

Usually I have a repo, so I hand the other tool a task summary and carry on. When Codex starts working badly, I switch back to Claude.

Honestly, I have a feeling they slightly dumb down the models once they have a base of people who won't leave right away.

So it's important to switch at the right time.

The good news: the line keeps moving. Before, in Cursor, everything broke after about 10 requests. Now you can work on code for weeks and it holds.

The only thing we stay loyal to is the deadline. Our sites ship in about 72 hours, and no model gets to slow that down.

author: Egor Galiy
headline: Team Lead Designer at übernatural · 400+ websites, 3 Awwwards
title: The 3D site with zero 3D in it
text:
A 3D forest on a website: three images, about 40 lines of code.
No 3D editor was opened.

When a client asks for a 3D site, most likely they just want a cool effect.

For me design is engineering. You pick the technology that gets the effect at the lowest cost.

So by default we fake it. We generate the scene as a photo and animate it into a video, tied to the scroll or the mouse.

A video can weigh more than a model, but it puts less load on the visitor's processor and memory.

For the forest, one photo plus a depth map and a normal map is enough, and the branches actually move under the mouse.

My first try took a couple of hours. Now it takes minutes. It's still a studio experiment, not client work yet.

Real 3D models are a luxury. We build them when there's a real need, a real budget and room to stretch the timeline.

Our whole project ships in a few days, so the budget goes where the visitor can see it.

title: The AI said 240 hours. It was 20.
text:
I asked an AI how much time our meeting bot saves us.
It said 240 hours a month. The real number is about 20.

It assumed every one of our 12 people sits in 2 to 4 calls a day. It's 2 to 4 calls a day for the whole team.

The bot itself is simple. Read AI records every daily meeting, Claude splits the transcript into tasks, and one Telegram button drops the checklist into the right Notion project.

About 250 meetings a month, around $0.02 each, just under $7 a month all-in.

Before, someone had to rewatch a call at 2x speed and write the tasks down by hand.

The part I care about is the energy. We took one whole process out of a person's life, and now the document just lands in their hands.

It's one of the small bots that keep a 12-person studio shipping sites in 72 hours.

author: Egor Galiy
headline: Team Lead Designer at übernatural · 400+ websites, 3 Awwwards
title: Three kinds of designers
text:
There are three kinds of designers right now.
Before AI, we sat in the middle of that pyramid.

People who know how to design. People who can vibe-code but can't design. And people who do both.

Before AI showed up, we were somewhere in the middle: the ones who know how to design, competing with everyone else who designs.

Then the order changed. Not everyone who used to rank above us switched to using the models.

So now we sit near the top, and we try to keep up with every model that matters.

You can tell right away when a person has never touched design before. Composition problems, style that drifts, the same overused templates I see every day.

A model can draw a decent-looking page now. I still point out its mistakes to it several times per page.

Someone who isn't into design doesn't see those mistakes, so they ship a product that isn't very good.

Every site we ship at übernatural goes through both halves: the model builds, a designer catches what it got wrong.

text:

It will never be perfect.

author: Egor Galiy
headline: Team Lead Designer at übernatural · 400+ websites, 3 Awwwards
title: Half of designers ship AI code
text:
Half of designers now say they've shipped AI-written code to a live product.
Most of them don't understand code.

That's from this year's AI in Design report: 900+ designers in 60+ countries. 91% use AI for design every week. A year earlier it was 54%.

To me this is more a question about code than about design. Designers use the code however the model spits it out, without much checking.

The first risk is legal. A form collects people's data, the designer has no idea about the laws, and they end up violating consumer rights without knowing it.

The second is security. If you don't know what's under the hood, your product is easier to hack.

In our studio, on projects that collect data, we build out all the legal pages and do everything by the law.

And we don't take projects with important databases. A serious one needs a whole separate person just for security, and that isn't the work we do.

If a fast, cheap site is about to collect your customers' data, ask who read the code.

author: Egor Galiy
headline: Team Lead Designer at übernatural · 400+ websites, 3 Awwwards
title: Framer: a design studio that became $2B
text:
Framer's founders ran a design studio before building a $2B company.
They sold that studio to Facebook in 2011.

Then Koen Bok and Jorn van Dijk built the website tool that studios like ours now ship on.

In August 2025 Framer raised $100M at a $2B valuation. At the time, 40% of Y Combinator's most recent batch had their sites on it.

We build in Framer every day, including with its AI. My honest split, from real builds:

Figma Make can do maybe 20% of a real website. It lays out blocks, but it can't make a nice looking design, and I have to clean up its layout.

Framer's AI works with Framer's actual features: animations, colour changes in the library, headers set up properly, decent responsiveness.

I can hand it 25 to 30% of the work, and while it works, I go do something else.

My hypothesis is that AI should eventually do 60 to 70% of a fast website. We're building the habit now so we're ready when it can.

The idea and the look stay with a person. That's the part you pay a studio for.

title: The client's calendar is the limit
text:
The fastest any service business can move is one client meeting a day

A founder or a head of marketing has a board, a product, a team, investors. To look at a website properly they need a clear hour, and most of them get one a day. More contact than that and the client starts working for the studio

So the real timeline is a count of sessions. Three sessions, three days, and we moved to three on purpose

Everything on our side is tuned to one target: get as much done as possible between two sessions. Quality stays fixed, speed is the variable

title: Dubai sold 132,000 unbuilt homes
text:
Dubai sold 132,000 homes in 2025 that did not exist yet

That's 65% of all residential sales in the city, worth AED 286 billion, against 71,000 finished homes resold (betterhomes, full-year 2025 report)

So two out of three homes sold last year were bought as a promise. A view nobody can stand in yet

Until the tower is finished, the buyer has a render, a brochure and a website. For two or three years, that is the product

Which changes the math on the website. On a nine-figure tower it's a rounding error in the budget. It's also the thing every buyer, broker and bank opens first, often from another continent

I'd file it under sales, next to the show apartment

One of our clients owns skyscrapers in New York. What I took from that work: the site's real job is to make a room that doesn't exist yet feel real

author: Bogdan Chechin
headline: Co-founder at übernatural · Websites for founders and enterprises
title: You can't sue a prompt
text:
You can't sue a prompt. Air Canada found out what happens when a company tries something close

Its website chatbot told a customer he could apply for a bereavement fare refund after the trip. The real policy said otherwise. When the customer claimed the money, the tribunal summed up the airline's position as treating the chatbot as "a separate legal entity that is responsible for its own actions"

The tribunal called it "a remarkable submission" and held the airline responsible for all the information on its website (Moffatt v. Air Canada, 2024)

That's my main argument for why companies will keep paying people and firms even when models do most of the work. Someone has to answer for the result, and a model can't

AI agents can already hold a bank card. Nobody has built them a way to carry a loss. My hunch is that one day a protocol will pool part of every agent's fees to cover exactly that. Until then, the liability sits with a human who has a name and a contract

For anyone buying a website, it's a boring point that matters. A fixed price, a fixed date, and someone who answers for both
comment:
The ruling, with the tribunal's quotes: https://www.mccarthy.ca/en/insights/blogs/techlex/moffatt-v-air-canada-misrepresentation-ai-chatbot

author: Bogdan Chechin
headline: Co-founder at übernatural · Websites for founders and enterprises
title: Lovable and the price of average
text:
Lovable is worth $13.3 billion. The product opened to the public in December 2024

60 million projects hosted. A $500 million annual revenue run rate by June 2026

In our market it's the clearest example of basic supply and demand. When the supply of something becomes almost infinite, its price falls toward zero. Anyone can now get a decent-looking website for the price of a subscription

We felt it directly. Most of the small clients who used to write to us now build it themselves

The bigger ones stayed. For a startup that raised $3M, a company selling towers or a team pitching a ministry, the website has one job: to look unlike the other 60 million before the first call

So the market split in two. Self-service at one end. At the other, people who want something far from average and would rather pay someone who does it well

Lovable is a great business. It's also the best argument I know for why outstanding design gets more expensive from here

author: Bogdan Chechin
headline: Co-founder at übernatural · Websites for founders and enterprises
title: Things buyers hear from agencies
text:
Things buyers hear before they ever see their website

The fear behind buying a website comes down to three things. Unpredictable results. Unpredictable timing. A bad experience last time

Every line in the picture is one of those three, said out loud

It matters more than it looks. 6sense surveyed more than 4,000 B2B buyers in 2025. 94% of buying groups had ranked a preferred vendor before the first contact, and they bought from that favourite 77% of the time

So most of the decision is made on what the buyer sees before anyone talks. The site, the work, whether the price is clear

That's why we skip the budget game. Fixed price, a date that doesn't move, and the portfolio says the rest

P. S. The picture is a joke. The 77% comes from more than 4,000 buyers

author: Bogdan Chechin
headline: Co-founder at übernatural · Websites for founders and enterprises
title: One hour, 1,000,000 users
text:
At 19 I built a Telegram bot in about an hour. Then we forgot about it for almost 3 years

A birthday bot. No marketing, no plan, no updates

When we finally opened the stats it had 110,000 users. All organic. We were properly stunned

We rebuilt it. It passed 1,000,000 users, growing by 10,000 to 20,000 a day, and the birthday "gift" broadcasts converted at about 2%

My read on why: a birthday is the one day people message their friends anyway. The bot sat exactly on that moment, so every user was a small ad for the next one

The hour of building was the smallest input in the whole story

Funded founders sometimes ask me what makes a product spread. After that bot my answer is short: find the moment your buyer already has, and sit right on it. I now look for the same moment in every website we launch
